destination: Interpret all supplied policy clauses together, distinguish format from permission and inspection from reproduction, apply the scope of exceptions without silently waiving other conditions, and give a justified answer to both source cases. No general legal doctrine, archival-history survey, or actual legal advice.
calibration: Earlier exchange: The learner can read ordinary prose, identify an explicit condition and its consequence, and order events in time. Asked whether permission to inspect necessarily includes permission to copy, they said they cannot tell without a rule. Asked whether a named exception waives every condition in a document, they said they do not know. They have no legal training or prior knowledge of these synthetic archive rules. They explicitly confirmed that only the supplied policy governs the exercise and that they want to understand and apply the whole attached note.
source:
SYNTHETIC ARCHIVE POLICY AND APPLICATION NOTE

1. A member may consult public records on weekdays from 09:00 to 17:00.
2. Original documents additionally require a supervised appointment. A supervisor may expressly approve an appointment outside the weekday hours in clause 1; this approval changes only the hours condition.
3. A document marked restricted additionally requires its holder's written consent. An emergency inspection order signed by the archivist can replace that consent for inspection only. Such an order never permits reproduction.
4. A digital copy is a different format of the same record. Digital access does not by itself remove a restriction or grant reproduction permission. Reproduction of any restricted record requires the holder's separate written reproduction permission.
5. Exceptions replace only the conditions they name; all other applicable conditions remain in force. A supervised appointment by itself is not an emergency inspection order.

Case A. A member has a supervised Sunday appointment expressly approved for that time. The record is a restricted original. The holder supplied no consent of either kind. The archivist signed an emergency inspection order. May the member inspect? May the member photograph it?

Case B. The same member instead requests a digital copy on Tuesday at 11:00. The record remains restricted, there is no emergency order for this request, and there is no holder consent. The member argues that digital format makes it a public record and that the earlier appointment is sufficient. Does the policy permit this access? Which conditions matter?

Task: explain both outcomes from the clauses, including why an exception to one condition does not waive an unrelated condition. Do not import external law.

tree.topic: Applying scoped exceptions in the synthetic archive policy

nodes.label: Archive access conditions, record format, and reproduction
nodes.explanation: Assume only that the learner can read ordinary prose, identify an explicit condition and consequence, and order events in time; no legal knowledge or archive conventions are assumed. Teach how to determine ordinary permission by separating the requested action, the record's stated status and format, and the conditions that apply together. Supply the policy's ordinary rules: a member may consult public records on weekdays from 09:00 to 17:00; an original additionally requires a supervised appointment; a record marked restricted additionally requires its holder's written consent. Teach that 'additionally' retains the other applicable conditions. Clause 4 says a digital copy is a different format of the same record: digital access neither removes a restriction nor grants reproduction permission. Distinguish inspection or consultation from reproduction, including photographing a document, and distinguish written consent to inspect a restricted record from the holder's separate written reproduction permission required for reproduction of any restricted record. Have the learner explain, for example, why a member with written inspection consent can consult a restricted digital record during the permitted hours yet still lacks permission to reproduce it, and diagnose why changing an original to digital format does not clear its restriction. Use only the supplied policy; exceptions and their effects are developed in the following lesson.

nodes.label: Scoped exceptions: deciding Cases A and B
nodes.explanation: Build on the established distinction between format and restricted status, between inspection and reproduction, and between cumulative access conditions and separate reproduction permission. Develop a method for applying an exception: identify its trigger and the exact condition it replaces, retain every other applicable condition, and justify the requested action against the resulting requirements. Supply the remaining policy statements in full substance: under clause 2 a supervisor may expressly approve a supervised appointment outside the weekday hours, changing only the hours condition; under clause 3 an emergency inspection order signed by the archivist can replace the holder's written consent for inspection only and never permits reproduction; clause 5 says exceptions replace only the conditions they name, all other applicable conditions remain in force, and a supervised appointment by itself is not an emergency inspection order. Work through the actual cases. In Case A a member has a supervised Sunday appointment expressly approved for that time, seeks a restricted original, has neither kind of holder consent, and has an archivist-signed emergency inspection order. Develop the reasoning that inspection is permitted: the appointment supplies supervision, express approval replaces the hours condition, and the order replaces inspection consent; photographing is prohibited because the separate written reproduction permission is absent. In Case B the same member requests a digital copy on Tuesday at 11:00; it remains restricted, with no emergency order for this request and no holder consent. Develop the reasoning that membership and the ordinary hours are satisfied but access is blocked by the missing inspection consent or its permitted replacement. Digital format does not make the record public; the original-document appointment requirement does not attach merely because this is the same record, and the earlier appointment supplies neither holder consent nor an emergency order. Any reproduction would also require separate written reproduction permission; do not infer that format alone determines whether an action is reproduction. Have the learner produce a clause-linked answer to both cases and independently explain a nearby change, such as why adding inspection consent in Case B would change access permission without authorizing reproduction. Keep the reasoning within these synthetic rules, with no external law.

tree.topic: Applying the synthetic archive policy to restricted originals and digital copies

nodes.label: Cumulative conditions for archive consultation
nodes.explanation: The learner should be able to turn clauses 1–3 into a set of conditions that must all hold for an ordinary consultation: membership and the stated weekday hours, a supervised appointment when consulting an original, and the holder's written consent when the record is restricted. Use a simple request to show why satisfying one condition leaves the others to be checked, and how 'additionally' makes a requirement cumulative. Assume only the calibrated ability to read explicit conditions in ordinary prose. Work initially without exceptions; digital format and reproduction permissions have their own nodes.

nodes.label: Separate permissions for inspection and reproduction
nodes.explanation: The learner should be able to classify inspecting a record and photographing it as different actions, then distinguish written consent to inspect a restricted record from the holder's separate written reproduction permission. Clauses 3–4 make the action covered by a permission essential: the ability to look does not establish permission to make a copy. Practice identifying what a stated permission actually authorizes without assuming additional authority. Assume ordinary reading only; leave the other access conditions and the operation of emergency orders to their respective nodes, and infer no reproduction rules beyond those supplied.

nodes.label: Record format and restriction status
nodes.explanation: The learner should be able to explain why a restricted original's digital version remains the same restricted record under clause 4. Treat original versus digital as a format distinction and public versus restricted as an access-status distinction; changing the former does not itself change the latter or supply a permission. Use an existing restricted record shown on paper and on a screen to practice keeping these properties separate. Assume only ordinary prose comprehension. This node establishes what digital format changes; checking a request's conditions and distinguishing inspection from reproduction are separate goals.

nodes.label: Condition-specific exceptions
nodes.explanation: The learner should be able to mark exactly which condition an exception replaces while retaining every other applicable condition. Starting with the cumulative access checks, apply the supervisor's express approval to the hours condition alone, then apply an archivist-signed emergency inspection order in place of holder consent for inspection alone. Use clauses 2, 3, and 5 to explain why neither approval supplies an unrelated requirement, why the order never permits reproduction, and why a supervised appointment is not itself an emergency order. Practice tracing each piece of evidence to its named condition and action; do not introduce exceptions or legal principles outside this note.

nodes.label: Restricted-original inspection under the Sunday exceptions
nodes.explanation: The learner should be able to justify both Case A answers clause by clause. The member has the supervised appointment required for an original; its express Sunday approval replaces the ordinary hours condition, and the signed emergency order replaces the missing holder consent for inspection. Those facts together permit inspection. Photographing is reproduction, for which the restricted record still requires the holder's separate written permission; none was supplied, and the emergency order expressly cannot provide it, so photography is not permitted. Have the learner identify the distinct role of each document and explain why either exception alone would leave another inspection condition unresolved. Keep the conclusion specific to the supplied facts.

nodes.label: Restricted digital access and the appointment argument
nodes.explanation: The learner should be able to reject both arguments in Case B and identify the conditions that decide the request. Membership and Tuesday at 11:00 satisfy the baseline membership and hours checks, but digital format preserves the restriction: inspection still needs the holder's written consent or a qualifying emergency inspection order, and this request has neither. The supervised-appointment requirement concerns consulting originals; the earlier appointment supplies neither consent nor an emergency order, and an hours exception does no work within ordinary weekday hours. Thus digital access is not permitted. Also distinguish consulting an existing digital copy from reproducing the record: if the request involves reproduction, the separate written reproduction permission is independently absent. Require a clause-based explanation of the denial without treating format, an appointment, or an earlier approval as a general waiver.

tree.topic: Applying the synthetic archive access and reproduction policy

nodes.label: Record format and restriction status
nodes.explanation: The learner can distinguish a record's format from its restriction status and track that status across a change of format. Use an original and a digital copy of the same restricted record to explain clause 4: digitization preserves the restriction and creates no permission by itself. Assume only ordinary prose and identification of explicit conditions. Practice classifying the two attributes; leave complete access decisions and the distinction between inspection and reproduction to the following nodes.

nodes.label: Inspection and reproduction permissions
nodes.explanation: The learner can identify whether a proposed act is inspection or reproduction and identify the written permission required for each act on a restricted record. Explain that looking at a record is inspection and photographing it is reproduction. Clause 3 requires the holder's written consent for restricted inspection, while clause 4 requires separate written reproduction permission for copying. Permission for inspection alone therefore does not establish permission to photograph. Assume only ordinary prose and condition-consequence reading; scheduling requirements and emergency substitutions come later.

nodes.label: Cumulative conditions for an archive request
nodes.explanation: The learner can assemble the applicable conditions for a request from its record attributes and intended act. Start with membership and the weekday 09:00–17:00 window in clause 1, add a supervised appointment for an original under clause 2, and add holder consent for a restricted record under clause 3. Keep the separate reproduction-permission requirement visible when copying is requested. Teach 'additionally' as accumulation: satisfying one condition leaves the others to be checked. Use ordinary requests within regular hours; defer replacement of conditions by exceptions to the next node.

nodes.label: Condition-specific exceptions
nodes.explanation: The learner can identify exactly which condition an exception replaces and retain every other applicable condition under clause 5. Apply this method to the two supplied mechanisms: a supervisor's express approval of an out-of-hours appointment changes only the hours condition, and an archivist-signed emergency inspection order replaces only the holder's consent for inspection. The latter never grants reproduction permission. Practice updating the existing checklist one condition at a time, including when both mechanisms operate together. Establish explicitly that a supervised appointment alone is not an emergency order; assume no legal doctrine beyond these clauses.

nodes.label: Inspection and photography of a restricted original
nodes.explanation: The learner can justify both answers to Case A by matching every relevant fact to the policy. Membership and the supervised appointment satisfy their conditions; the supervisor's express Sunday approval replaces the regular-hours condition, and the signed emergency inspection order replaces the missing holder consent for inspection. Inspection is therefore permitted. Photography remains impermissible because the holder supplied no separate written reproduction permission and neither exception supplies it. Have the learner explain why the two successful exceptions cannot be extended to this remaining requirement, using only the supplied clauses.

nodes.label: Consent requirements for restricted digital access
nodes.explanation: The learner can reject both arguments in Case B and give a complete condition-based access decision. The member's Tuesday 11:00 request meets the ordinary membership and hours conditions, but the digital record remains restricted and lacks both holder consent for inspection and an emergency order replacing it, so access is denied. The digital copy does not itself trigger clause 2's appointment requirement for original documents; the earlier appointment cannot supply consent or become an emergency order. If fulfilling the request involves reproduction, separate written reproduction permission is also required. Distinguish viewing a digital record from reproducing it, and ground each conclusion in clauses 1–5.

tree.topic: Inspection, digital access, and reproduction under the synthetic archive policy

nodes.label: Ordinary archive permissions
nodes.explanation: Assume ordinary prose reading, recognition of an explicit condition and its consequence, and the ability to place events within stated days and hours; assume no legal training or knowledge of archive rules. The supplied synthetic policy is the sole authority. Develop the ability to distinguish a record's restriction status, its original or digital format, and the action requested, then identify all applicable ordinary permission conditions. Supply these rules: a member may consult public records on weekdays from 09:00 to 17:00; original documents additionally require a supervised appointment; a document marked restricted additionally requires its holder's written consent. Teach that “additionally” accumulates conditions, so restricted inspection retains the member and time conditions and, for an original, the supervised appointment condition. Also supply clause 4: a digital copy is a different format of the same record; digital access does not by itself remove a restriction or grant reproduction permission; reproduction of any restricted record requires the holder's separate written reproduction permission. Use an ordinary weekday request to develop a condition checklist, keeping inspection and reproduction decisions distinct. Explain why changing a restricted record to digital format does not make it public, why the original-document appointment requirement does not apply merely because a digital copy represents the same record, and why permission to inspect does not establish permission to photograph, which reproduces the record. Enable the learner to diagnose a request with inspection consent but no reproduction permission and to justify which conditions follow from format, restriction, and action. Special exceptions and the two source cases are left to the next lesson.

nodes.label: Limited exceptions in Cases A and B
nodes.explanation: Build on the ordinary condition checklist and the distinction between inspection consent and separate written reproduction permission. Teach the remaining source rules explicitly: a supervisor may expressly approve a supervised appointment outside the weekday hours of clause 1, and this approval changes only the hours condition; an emergency inspection order signed by the archivist can replace the holder's written consent for inspection only and never permits reproduction. Clause 5 states, “Exceptions replace only the conditions they name; all other applicable conditions remain in force,” and a supervised appointment by itself is not an emergency inspection order. Develop the reasoning by marking each ordinary condition as satisfied, expressly replaced, or still unmet, and matching approvals to the current request rather than treating them as general waivers. Apply this method to the complete source cases. In Case A, a member has a supervised Sunday appointment expressly approved for that time, seeks a restricted original, has no holder consent of either kind, and has an emergency inspection order signed by the archivist. Derive that inspection is permitted: membership and supervision are present, express approval replaces the ordinary hours condition, and the signed order replaces inspection consent. Derive separately that photography is forbidden because the holder's separate written reproduction permission is absent and the emergency order never authorizes reproduction. In Case B, the same member instead requests a digital copy on Tuesday at 11:00; the record remains restricted, there is no emergency order for this request, and there is no holder consent. Derive that the requested access is not permitted: membership and ordinary hours are satisfied, digital format preserves the restriction, and neither required inspection consent nor its authorized replacement is present. The original-specific appointment condition is not triggered by digital access, and the earlier appointment supplies neither holder consent nor an emergency order. Keep the denial of digital access grounded in the missing inspection authorization; if reproduction is also requested, separate written reproduction permission is an additional unsatisfied requirement. Enable the learner to explain why fixing one missing condition need not resolve another, and to refute the claims that digital means public or that an appointment supplies every needed permission. Finish with justified answers to both cases under these clauses alone; do not import external law or require proof of the supplied policy.
